buckets.title: Rational and real number inclusion — NCERT pilot
buckets.topic: Number Systems: rational numbers and real numbers
buckets.badge_reason: Identify the correct superset, not a subset that excludes negative or fractional rational values

conventions.statement: A rational number is a/b for integers a and b with b nonzero.
Every rational number is real; not every real number is rational.

capabilities.action: Classify a rational number as belonging to the real-number set, and reject narrower categories when the statement says every.
capabilities.success_criterion: State Q ⊆ R and supply a counterexample to the claims that all rationals are natural numbers, integers or whole numbers.

microtopics.title: Every rational number is real
microtopics.badge_reason: The quantifier every requires testing both fractional and negative rational values.
entry_assumptions: Distinguish integers from fractions with nonzero denominators.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Use Q ⊆ R as an inclusion relation, not the false reverse inclusion R ⊆ Q.

teaching_path.action: Define rational numbers as quotients a/b of integers with b nonzero.
teaching_path.why_valid: Every such quotient is a real number on the number line.
teaching_path.output: Any rational belongs to the real numbers.

teaching_path.action: Test the narrower claims with -1/2, 1/2 and -2.
teaching_path.why_valid: These are rational, but not all are whole, natural or integer values.
teaching_path.output: Reject natural number, integer and whole number as universal classifications.

teaching_path.action: Identify the real-number set as a valid universal superset of the rational numbers.
teaching_path.why_valid: The set inclusion Q ⊆ R establishes option C without claiming R ⊆ Q.
teaching_path.output: Every rational number is a real number.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every rational number is an integer because it is a quotient of integers.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Is 1/2 an integer? Can 1/2 be written as a/b with integers a and b ≠ 0?
misconceptions.repair: A quotient of integers need not be an integer; rationals include non-integer fractions.

exit_task.prompt: Is -3/2 rational and real? Is every real number rational? Justify both claims.

answer.summary: -3/2 is a rational number and thus a real number. Not every real number is rational: √2 is real but irrational.
reasoning: Write -3/2 as a quotient of integers with nonzero denominator.
Use √2 to refute the reverse inclusion.
answer.check: One rational counterexample disproves a narrower universal claim, while √2 disproves real ⊆ rational.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: This exit task tests definitions and a set-inclusion proof, not a computed numerical answer.

microtopics.research_contribution: Issue #131 TEST product specimen selected from independently reconciled NCERT Number Systems Q1; no curriculum admission is implied.

construction_units.decision: Distinguish a universal containing set from narrower alternatives using a rational counterexample.

independent_checks.statement: Use 1/2: it is rational and real, but not integer, whole or natural. Therefore three narrower universal choices fail.
Use √2 to disprove the converse: a real number need not be rational.

relations.meaning: Every rational number is also a real number; the reverse inclusion does not hold.

symbols.meaning: Set of rational numbers a/b with integers a,b and b nonzero
Set of real numbers on the number line
Is a subset of; the left set is contained in the right set

conditions: A rational number has the form a/b with integer numerator and nonzero integer denominator.
The real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers.

derivation.action: Take any rational x. By definition x=a/b for integers a,b, with b nonzero.
derivation.why_valid: This is the definition of the rational-number set.
derivation.output: x is a quotient of integers with nonzero denominator.

derivation.action: Locate the quotient a/b on the real number line.
Test 1/2 against the narrower options and √2 against the converse.
derivation.why_valid: One counterexample refutes a universal statement.

limits: This does not assert that every real number is rational.
The notation is the author's symbolic explanation, not an additional quoted NCERT condition.
checks: 1/2 is rational and real, but is not an integer, whole number or natural number.
√2 is real and irrational; reversing the inclusion is incorrect.

question_families.title: Recognise the inclusion of rational numbers in real numbers
solution_structure: Define a rational number as an integer quotient.
Check the universal quantifier using rational counterexamples to narrower options.
Conclude every rational belongs to the real-number set.

demand_dimensions.novelty: Requires separating a set from its subsets

safe_variations: Test a negative rational and a non-integral fraction.
transfer_boundaries: Do not infer that every real number is rational.
common_wrong_routes: Calling every rational an integer because numerator and denominator are integers.
